explanations.answer: Be careful not to pass by that place
explanations.explanation: Elisha, the man of God, sends word to the king of Israel: "Be careful not to pass by this place, for the Arameans are going down there." (2 Kings 6:9) It's a warning, plain and simple. Aram picks the spot and Elisha tells Israel to steer clear of it.

explanations.answer: Set up your own camp there first
explanations.explanation: That's not in the message, friend. Elisha doesn't tell the king to go claim the spot. He says, "Be careful not to pass by this place…" (2 Kings 6:9) Walking toward a place you were just warned about is like ignoring a sign that says wet paint and touching it to be sure.

explanations.answer: Attack that place before they arrive
explanations.explanation: No battle plan here. Elisha doesn't say a word about attacking. The message is a caution: "Be careful not to pass by this place, for the Arameans are going down there." (2 Kings 6:9) Then the king sends word to that place and stays on his guard (2 Kings 6:10).

The text says the opposite. "So the king of Israel sent word to the place the man of God had pointed out." (2 Kings 6:10) He didn't ignore Elisha, he acted on the warning. The text says Elisha warned him time and again, so the king "…was on his guard in such places."

That's right, the king doesn't ignore it. He sends word to the place the man of God pointed out. (2 Kings 6:10) Elisha warns him time and again, and the king stays on his guard in those places. I think that's a king who is paying attention.

The king of Aram is enraged and asks his servants, "Tell me, which one of us is on the side of the king of Israel?" (2 Kings 6:11) He thinks the leak is somebody in his own camp. It's like the cookies keep vanishing and you start side-eyeing the whole kitchen.

explanations.answer: Scouts from Israel on the hills
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the king never mentions scouts. He asks his own servants, "…which one of us is on the side of the king of Israel?" (2 Kings 6:11) That word "us" tells you he's looking inside his own camp.

Merchants don't come up anywhere in this passage. The king of Aram calls his servants and demands, "Tell me, which one of us is on the side of the king of Israel?" (2 Kings 6:11) He suspects someone on his own side.

The servant says Elisha tells the king of Israel "…the very words you speak in your bedroom." (2 Kings 6:12) That's the one room where you figure nobody's listening. Elisha, the prophet in Israel, somehow knows it all anyway.

Close, but that's not the word. The servant says "…the very words you speak in your bedroom." (2 Kings 6:12) A courtyard is out in the open. I bet a bedroom is the last place a king expects anyone to hear him.
The servant doesn't say temple. The text says Elisha tells the king of Israel "…the very words you speak in your bedroom." (2 Kings 6:12) That's about as private as a king's talking gets.
The report comes in: "Elisha is in Dothan…" (2 Kings 6:13) The king of Aram wanted to know where Elisha was so he could send men to capture him. Now he has a spot on the map.
Jericho isn't the answer here. The report says, "Elisha is in Dothan…" (2 Kings 6:13) That's the place the king of Aram sends horses, chariots, and a great army. (2 Kings 6:14)

Bethel isn't the answer here. The report to the king of Aram says, "Elisha is in Dothan…" (2 Kings 6:13) The king wanted to know where Elisha was so he could send men to capture him. Dothan is where his army heads.
The king of Aram sends "…horses, chariots, and a great army." (2 Kings 6:14) That's a lot of force headed for one man of God. I think that king wasn't taking any chances.
A caravan sounds like a road trip with snacks, and this was no road trip. The king sends "…horses, chariots, and a great army." (2 Kings 6:14) These men came to capture Elisha.
A procession sounds like a parade, and nobody's throwing confetti here. The text says the king sent "…horses, chariots, and a great army." (2 Kings 6:14) They went by night and surrounded the city.

Yes, the servant sees the army and says, "Oh, my master, what are we to do?" (2 Kings 6:15) He gets up early, steps outside, and there they are, horses and chariots all around the city. I think I'd be asking the same question.

It's actually true. The servant of the man of God goes out early in the morning, sees the army, and asks Elisha, "Oh, my master, what are we to do?" (2 Kings 6:15) The servant doesn't stay quiet about it.

explanations.answer: There are more with us than with them
explanations.explanation: Elisha says, "Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them." (2 Kings 6:16) The army outside is easy to see, and Elisha is pointing to something that isn't. His reason is about who is with them.

explanations.answer: The army will leave before night
explanations.explanation: Elisha never says the army is leaving. His reason is, "…those who are with us are more than those who are with them." (2 Kings 6:16) He's not promising the army will go away. He's telling his servant who is on their side.

explanations.answer: The city walls are too strong for them
explanations.explanation: Walls don't come up in Elisha's answer at all. He says, "Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them." (2 Kings 6:16) His comfort isn't about stone. It's about who is standing with them.

The LORD opens the young man's eyes, and he sees that "…the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha." (2 Kings 6:17) Earlier he had seen an army with horses and chariots surrounding the city. (2 Kings 6:15) Now he sees what Elisha meant.

Naaman was an Aramean commander in another story (2 Kings 5:1), but he's not in this scene. The hills are full of horses and chariots of fire "…all around Elisha." (2 Kings 6:17) Elisha is the one who stands in the middle of it.

Hazael, who later reigns over Aram (2 Kings 8:15), isn't named in this passage. The young man sees the hills full of horses and chariots of fire "…all around Elisha." (2 Kings 6:17) That's the one the fire surrounds.

Elisha prays to the LORD, "Please strike these people with blindness." (2 Kings 6:18) The Arameans are coming down against him, and that's his request. Then the text says, "So He struck them with blindness, according to the word of Elisha."
The chariots of fire were on the hills around Elisha, but he doesn't ask for fire to fall. His prayer is, "Please strike these people with blindness." (2 Kings 6:18) Blindness is the answer.

explanations.answer: Put them into a deep sleep
explanations.explanation: Sleep sounds gentle, but that's not what he asks. Elisha prays, "Please strike these people with blindness." (2 Kings 6:18) The Arameans can't see, but they're still on their feet and can still be led.

That's right. Elisha tells them, "This is not the way, and this is not the city." (2 Kings 6:19) He says it after the LORD struck them with blindness. (2 Kings 6:18) Then he tells them to follow him and says he will take them to the man they are seeking.
It's actually true. Elisha tells the blinded Arameans, "This is not the way, and this is not the city." (2 Kings 6:19) Then he tells them to follow him.

The text says, "And he led them to Samaria." (2 Kings 6:19) Elisha had told them, "Follow me…" The Arameans were blind the whole walk. Then once they entered Samaria, the LORD opened their eyes. (2 Kings 6:20)
Damascus isn't where this walk ends. The text says Elisha "…led them to Samaria." (2 Kings 6:19) Samaria is the city where they open their eyes.

Gilgal's a fair guess, friend, but it never shows up in this passage. Elisha leads the blinded Arameans to Samaria. (2 Kings 6:19) Picture the walk: a whole army following one man who says, "Follow me…" and they just DO it! Then the LORD opens their eyes, and they look around and find out they're in Samaria. (2 Kings 6:20) I bet that was a SURPRISE!
Elisha prays, "O LORD, open the eyes of these men that they may see." (2 Kings 6:20) Then the LORD opens their eyes. They look around and discover they're in Samaria.

Their ears were working fine, since they could hear Elisha say, "Follow me." (2 Kings 6:19) What he asks for is, "…open the eyes of these men that they may see." (2 Kings 6:20) Eyes are what had been struck.
Hearts are a nice guess, but the text doesn't say that. Elisha prays, "O LORD, open the eyes of these men that they may see." (2 Kings 6:20) He's undoing the blindness from earlier.

The king of Israel asks Elisha, "My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?" (2 Kings 6:21) He asks Elisha before he does anything. I think that says something about who he trusts to give the answer.

explanations.answer: Whether he should keep them as servants
explanations.explanation: Servants never come up in the king's question. He asks, "My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?" (2 Kings 6:21) The king is asking about their lives.

explanations.answer: Whether he should send them back blind
explanations.explanation: The Arameans' eyes were already opened by then. (2 Kings 6:20) The king asks, "My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?" (2 Kings 6:21) It's a much heavier question.
The text says the opposite. Elisha answers, "Do not kill them…" (2 Kings 6:22) He goes further and tells the king to feed them.
That's right. Elisha says, "Do not kill them…" (2 Kings 6:22) Then he asks the king whether he would kill those he had captured with his own sword or bow. Elisha's answer to the king is no.

explanations.answer: Set food and water before them
explanations.explanation: Elisha says, "Set food and water before them, that they may eat and drink and then return to their master." (2 Kings 6:22) These men came to capture him. Now they're getting a meal.

explanations.answer: Lock them up in the city prison
explanations.explanation: No prison anywhere in Elisha's answer. After saying not to kill them, he says, "Set food and water before them, that they may eat and drink and then return to their master." (2 Kings 6:22) They're headed home, not behind bars.

explanations.answer: Make them work on the city walls
explanations.explanation: Elisha doesn't hand out any jobs. He says, "Set food and water before them, that they may eat and drink and then return to their master." (2 Kings 6:22) Walls never come up at all.

The text says, "So the king prepared a great feast for them…" (2 Kings 6:23) Elisha only said to set out food and water, and the king goes big. After they finish eating and drinking, he sends them away.
No courtroom here. The king of Israel "…prepared a great feast for them…" (2 Kings 6:23) A trial would be a very different afternoon.

Nobody's marching anywhere yet. The king "…prepared a great feast for them…" and only after they finish eating and drinking does he send them away. (2 Kings 6:23) The feast comes before the trip home.

That's right. The passage ends, "And the Aramean raiders did not come into the land of Israel again." (2 Kings 6:23) Before that, the king prepared a great feast for them and sent them away, and they returned to their master. Then the raiders stop coming.
It's actually true. The last line says, "And the Aramean raiders did not come into the land of Israel again." (2 Kings 6:23) They go back to their master, and the raids stop.
